title: Game Awards
principle: Celebrate others' success without tearing other games down
why: Awards work best as a way for creators and fans to celebrate and spread happiness; raising one thing up doesn't mean bringing everything around it down.
how: Frame recognition as celebration of the team's hard work and of good games, not as a race.
anti_pattern: Treating awards as a race.
quote: Raising one thing up doesn't mean bringing everything around it down in the process.

title: Just Let Them Play!
principle: Show real gameplay early in trailers
why: Many trailers open with long story sequences and he skips ahead; people can't be expected to buy a game if they can't tell what kind of game it is.
how: Put gameplay footage near the start and save high-end CG movies and openings for later.
anti_pattern: Trailers that open with story.
example: Game trailers on online storefronts.
quote: Save the high-end CG movies and openings for later.

title: Super Smash Bros.
principle: Give players a reason to care about a large cast immediately.
why: Console fighting games can launch with 8 or even 12 new main characters at once, and it's hard to make someone care about them.
how: Use characters players already know, or build ways for attachment to grow, as arcades do through watching others play.
anti_pattern: A roster full of characters nobody has seen.
example: Smash borrowing Nintendo's most popular characters.
quote: For the customer, that's 12 new faces who just showed up out of nowhere.

title: The Price of Games
principle: Weigh subscription deals: covered costs versus competing with older titles.
why: Subscriptions bring the joy of having production costs covered, but also the pain of competing with older titles in the same catalog.
how: When deciding whether to release through a subscription service, count both the cost coverage and the competition from the back catalog.
quote: There's the joy of having your production costs covered, but also the pain of competing with older titles.

title: My Feline Friend, Fukurashi
principle: When followers keep asking for something, give them dedicated content.
why: Followers of his daily Smash Bros. screens kept begging for more of his cat, so he devoted a whole video to her.
how: Note recurring requests from your audience, even off-topic ones, and answer them with a dedicated post or video.
example: His daily Smash Bros. screens on Twitter, where people asked for more cat posts.
quote: All that time I spent posting daily Smash Bros. screens on Twitter, there was one thing people begged me to post even more of.

title: Competing with the Past
principle: Count past titles as competition for your players' time
why: For the audience, time spent on something old is worth the same as time spent on something new, so the whole back catalog is competition.
how: When positioning a game, list the older games, ports and other media competing for the same player's time, not just this year's releases.
anti_pattern: Assuming your only competition is other new releases.
example: Subscription video services pit new films against decades of past titles.
quote: From the viewer's perspective, the time spent watching something new is of equal value to time spent watching something old.

title: Marketing is Multiplicative
principle: Treat making the game known as important as making it good
why: Development and marketing spin on the same axle; the success of one is proportional to the other, and with 10,000+ Steam releases in 2021 nobody finds games by chance.
how: From early in development, plan what the dev team will contribute to promotion, such as reveal trailers or an official info site.
anti_pattern: Assuming a good game will be discovered on its own.
example: Smash Bros. fighter reveal movies and the Smash Bros. Dojo site.
quote: An unknown game may as well not exist.

title: Marketing is Multiplicative
principle: Create in-game assets so they can double as marketing material
why: He always considers that assets like fighter artwork may be used outside the game as well.
how: Produce key art, renders and cinematics at a quality and format that marketing can reuse.
example: Smash Bros. fighter artwork.
quote: When creating assets like fighter artwork needed for the game itself, I always consider that it may be used elsewhere outside the game as well.

title: Marketing is Multiplicative
principle: Get the marketing plan and review official updates before posting
why: He asks publishers for marketing and operations details so he can suggest ideas, and checks every official social and website update.
how: Request the marketing and operations schedule and set up a review step for official posts.
anti_pattern: Flooding your personal account with announcements, which can rub people the wrong way.
quote: I don't personally write the updates that appear on the game's official Twitter account or the website, but I always check them over and offer feedback.

title: Paint an Accurate Picture of Your Game
principle: Make every marketing image match how the game actually feels
why: If the game's image and reality don't match, you fail to reach the people it would resonate with and disappoint those misled into buying it.
how: Check the title, box art, screenshots and trailers against actual play and fix anything that sets the wrong expectation.
anti_pattern: Painting a misleading picture just to surprise players, like a banana that tastes like an apple.
quote: No matter how much you want to catch your players by surprise, don't paint a picture that doesn't represent your game!

title: Paint an Accurate Picture of Your Game
principle: Choose a title that abbreviates into something memorable
why: Super Smash Bros. can become just "Smash," which may help people remember it more easily.
how: While naming, list the short forms players will likely use and prefer names that shorten well.
example: Super Smash Bros. → "Smash."

title: Paint an Accurate Picture of Your Game
principle: Subvert expectations only if it still captures the game's heart
why: Kirby Super Star's simple wooden-box cover seemed unrelated to the vibrant game but got straight to the heart of it; still, showing the game for what it is works better.
how: Use indirect or surprising packaging sparingly, and make sure it conveys the core feeling of the game.
example: Kirby Super Star (Japan): wooden-box cover proposed by Shigesato Itoi.
quote: There's a time and place for subverting expectations, but the more effective strategy is to show your game for what it truly is.

title: Branching Tastes
principle: Pick your target from a top-down market view, not taste
why: Players' styles have diversified widely, so relying on your own likes and dislikes misreads the market.
how: Map current player segments and deliberately choose which one your game serves.
anti_pattern: Choosing a target audience from personal preference alone.
quote: The more aware you are of the market, the better you'll be able to target it— and that's really the main point here.

title: Branching Tastes
principle: For broad hits, aim at the shared tastes of young players
why: Values branch apart as people age, so the market is broadest at the trunk, before everyone finds their own branch; orthodox games and series fit values many players hold dear.
how: Use orthodox, broadly appealing design and create era-appropriate successors so enthusiasm passes to the next generation.
example: Nintendo's top sellers being hits with younger generations.
quote: In a world full of diverse tastes, the market is broadest at the stage before everyone finds their own branch.

title: Branching Tastes
principle: Target a niche branch deliberately for devoted fans
why: Aiming a game directly at one branch might make its players really fall in love with it, so not every game has to target the trunk.
how: If you go niche, commit to that branch's values instead of hedging toward everyone.

title: Game Demos
principle: Budget a demo as a separate small game, not a quick slice
why: From the moment you decide on a demo you maintain two versions with separate management, updates, tuning and QA, and anything public needs nearly final-level testing.
how: Schedule the demo as its own deliverable with its own tuning, update and QA passes.
anti_pattern: Assuming a demo is just a piece carved off the full game.
quote: If you're not careful, it can be almost like creating another small game.

title: Game Demos
principle: Only release a demo balanced enough to represent the final game
why: A half-baked demo increases the risk of players writing you off, and negative word of mouth turns away potential players.
how: If the pre-release build isn't balanced, consider a post-launch demo made from the finished game, accepting a smaller splash.
anti_pattern: Rushing out an unbalanced demo on the idea that something is better than nothing.

title: Game Demos
principle: Work to make your game known; demos are highly effective
why: Most games go unnoticed and publicity alone usually isn't enough; downloadable demos may be more effective than ever.
how: Weigh a demo early in your marketing plan, deciding between pre-launch impact and post-launch ease.
quote: Still, demos can be very effective, and in the end, it's absolutely better to be known than to be unknown.

title: Official Websites
principle: Keep an official website as the home base for all game information
why: People dig into websites less now that social media delivers short bursts, but a game still needs one place that delivers all its information.
how: Maintain one canonical site, review its layout and every update yourself, and run it alongside a blog and official social accounts.
anti_pattern: Scattering information only across social posts.
example: Smash Ultimate's site, which Sakurai helps lay out and checks with every update.
quote: In the end, it's still important to have a place to deliver all your information.

title: Official Websites
principle: Structure your site around your game's content, not a standard template
why: Smash has a huge variety of elements, so its site goes in depth to match, holding far more than the average game site.
how: Build sections from your actual content (characters, modes, techniques, online, stages, music, events) and add features the game needs, like a music player.
anti_pattern: A generic site made "in a standard fashion."
example: Smash Ultimate's site: fighters, 100+ stages, Pokémon and Assist Trophies, music player, fighter reveals, tournaments.
quote: Instead of just making a site in a standard fashion, you want to find a form that best fits your game.

title: Official Websites
principle: When others misread your game, explain its push and pull yourself
why: A game unlike anything before runs into preconceptions. Magazines ignored Sakurai's documentation, so he built his own channel, and proactively finding new solutions paid off later.
how: Write a clear guide to how your game plays and where its depth lies, and publish it yourself if press won't.
anti_pattern: Waiting for press or partners to discover your game's depth.
example: Smash Bros. DOJO!!, the players' guide site Sakurai hand-coded for the original Smash Bros.
quote: In challenging situations like that, proactively searching for new solutions will ultimately prove fruitful in the future.

title: Show and Tell: Some Rare Belongings
principle: When filming solo without zoom, cut to close-up photos and video
why: Sakurai shot the video alone and couldn't zoom while talking, so he cut to close-ups to show the details.
how: Shoot close-up photos or clips of small details in advance and edit them in.
quote: I can't zoom in while I'm talking, so I'll cut to close-up photos and videos instead.

title: Do Graphics Impact Fun?
principle: Make visuals strong enough to draw players in on crowded storefronts
why: On stores like Steam, people use a game's banner to decide whether to look at it. If the visuals don't draw them in, they won't play.
how: Treat banner and key art as critical assets and test whether they make people want to click.
anti_pattern: Assuming good gameplay will be found regardless of presentation.
example: Steam's almost endless lineup.
quote: If your visuals don't draw players in, people won't play your game.

title: Avoiding Comparison
principle: Check that your audience shares a reference before using it
why: Comparisons mean different things depending on generation and experience; 'Mario' can mean the NES game, Mario Odyssey or just the character.
how: Use comparisons only when the situation and listener make them helpful, and never measure by your own play history alone.
anti_pattern: Assuming your own gaming history is everyone's reference point.
example: 'Mario' — Super Mario Bros. on the NES vs. Mario Odyssey vs. the character
quote: Every generation has different knowledge and different sensibilities, so it's best not to measure things based on your own personal experiences.

title: Fighter Reveal Videos
principle: Lock a trailer's structure and length with animatics before CG production
why: Fighter reveals move from Sakurai's plot (cuts, character behavior, music cues) to storyboards to animatics, at which point the video's structure and length are essentially set before CG production begins.
how: Write a cut-by-cut plot, storyboard it, then make an animatic by moving and stretching storyboard art and approve its timing before any final rendering.
example: Super Smash Bros. — fighter reveal production pipeline
quote: At this point, the video's structure and length are essentially set.

title: Fighter Reveal Videos
principle: When a shot feels good enough, zoom in and go bolder
why: Sakurai's most frequent notes on reveal footage were to push past 'good enough': bolder framing, a changed angle of view, more interaction between fighters, a balance of serious and comical, and syncing to music.
how: Run each trailer shot through those checks: zoom in, change the angle of view, add interactions, balance serious and comic beats, cut to the music.
anti_pattern: Settling for safe, adequate framing.
example: Super Smash Bros. — fighter reveal gameplay segments
quote: When you think something's good enough, zoom in and go bolder.

title: Show the Actual Game!
principle: Always ship a trailer that shows the actual game
why: Nearly every game has a promotional video, and Sakurai won't buy a game without one unless there's a very good reason.
how: Treat a gameplay trailer as a required deliverable, including on your store page.
anti_pattern: Store-page trailers with no gameplay footage at all.
example: Some Steam page trailers show no gameplay.

title: Show the Actual Game!
principle: Show gameplay as soon as possible in every trailer
why: Long logos and intros make viewers skip ahead, and trailers exist to show what the game is about; a trailer will never be on the level of a film.
how: Cut opening logos, movies and character intros, lead with what makes the game appealing, and leave story and world for later.
anti_pattern: Opening movies and character intros that take forever to reach gameplay.
quote: And please, get to the actual game as soon as possible!

title: Show the Actual Game!
principle: Rely on teasers only if your name already sells
why: Popular series and famous creators can get by with teasers, but new IP, especially indie titles, must show gameplay to be understood.
how: For a new or indie title, open with gameplay, footage that illustrates the systems, or an honest tech demo of how the game really runs.
anti_pattern: Teaser-only reveals for a new IP.

title: Competition and Abundance
principle: Benchmark your game against past classics, not only new releases
why: Games take many hours to play, so every developer competes for player time, and subscription services make competition with past titles unavoidable.
how: Before committing to a commercial project, list the old and new games your target player could play instead, and define why they would choose yours.
anti_pattern: Assuming your game will find players just because you think it is fun.
example: Subscription services placing older catalog titles beside new releases.
quote: Remember, you're not only competing against the latest titles, but those created in the past as well.

title: Playing Games in Front of Other People
principle: Plan demos to show every key feature in close matches
why: Showing a game directly is probably the most effective form of presentation, so the goal is to capture as much quality footage as possible.
how: Make a checklist of all special moves, the super move and as many regular moves as possible, and keep matches relatively close.
anti_pattern: Demoing without understanding the game's content.
example: Mr. Sakurai Presents: Sakurai played each DLC fighter himself, using all of its special moves and its Final Smash.
quote: To put it simply, I'm always trying to get as much quality footage as I can.

title: Targeting and Market Research
principle: Don't let market research generate your new game ideas
why: Research is built on finished products and only shows the safe main road; following it makes work more average and mediocre, and it sells less.
how: Form the concept first and use data only to check risks; ask what a booming genre will look like when you release.
anti_pattern: Chasing whatever genre the data says is selling now.
example: Around the NES-to-SNES transition, many Japanese companies made Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy-like RPGs and dove into an overcrowded market.
quote: Targeting and market research data is built on everything that's come before. They don't show the path to what comes next.

title: Targeting and Market Research
principle: Target players by experience level, not by age or gender
why: Audience lines are blurry: some older people like cute things and some kids prefer intense content, and "beginners" spans all ages and genders.
how: Define the audience by need (e.g., beginners) and still give the controls enough depth that advanced players enjoy them.
anti_pattern: Treating demographic slices as hard boundaries.
example: The original Kirby was designed for beginners, never "for children", yet advanced players enjoy how it controls.
quote: So if I had to name a target audience, it would be "beginners." Not any specific age range.

title: Gameplay as Part of a Live Performance
principle: Keep real failure stakes when showing gameplay to a live audience
why: The chance that a Game Over would end the performance with no restart made it a one-of-a-kind thrill, and audience feedback said exactly that.
how: Play at high difficulty with no restarts so the audience senses genuine risk, as Sakurai did at Intensity 9.0 with zero defense.
example: PRESS START 2012: Kid Icarus: Uprising Chapter 12 Air Battle played live with the orchestra.
quote: The heart and soul of PRESS START is that everything was done live. It was meant to be enjoyed there alone.

title: Online Updates
principle: Ship in the best possible shape; patches can't recover lost players
why: No matter how much a game improves through patches, it means nothing if players have already given up on it.
how: Set your release quality bar as if no update will come.
anti_pattern: Shipping rough and planning to fix it later.
quote: no matter how much you improve your game through patches, it won't mean anything if your players have already given up on the game.

title: Online Updates
principle: Fix crash bugs first; treat balance and QoL patches as optional
why: Fatal bugs must be fixed, but balance tweaks and quality-of-life features are a free bonus that ties up the director and key staff who could start the next game.
how: Triage post-launch work by severity and weigh optional updates against freeing the core team.

title: Smash Bros. DOJO!!
principle: Explain a misunderstood game's essence directly to players
why: The original Smash's rules, controls and feel were unlike earlier fighting games, so people dismissed it before release, and a document sent to magazines had little impact.
how: Write a plain guide to the game's essence and unique features and publish it directly to players.
anti_pattern: Relying only on press coverage to explain an unusual game.
example: Sakurai turned "The Secrets of Smash Bros." into the Smash Bros. DOJO!! site, built himself in an HTML editor.

title: Smash Bros. DOJO!!
principle: Post updates on a fixed, frequent schedule fans can rely on
why: People came to the site excited to see something new, which works well once it becomes a daily routine.
how: Release one new detail on a set schedule (e.g., every weekday) and plan localization early for a global audience.
example: Smash Bros. Brawl's Dojo posted five times a week in six languages.

title: Smash Bros. DOJO!!
principle: Have the person who knows the game best shape its messaging
why: The director knows the content and its fun best; delegating still means briefing on every post and reviewing it.
how: Delegate production tasks like screenshots, but have the director write or review public explanations.
example: During Melee's brutal development, Sakurai updated the Dojo himself and replied to comments.

title: Smash Bros. DOJO!!
principle: Treat development and marketing as equally necessary parts of shipping
why: No matter how good a game is, nobody plays it if nobody knows about it, and today information has to reach people scrolling social media.
how: Plan how each piece of news will reach players' feeds alongside development milestones.
anti_pattern: Treating marketing as separate from development.
example: Mr. Sakurai Presents videos are another way he delivers information.
quote: I see development and marketing as two wheels on one axle. No matter how good something is, an unknown game might as well not exist.

title: Be Mindful of the Time Players are Giving You
principle: Give your game enough appeal to beat low-effort phone content
why: Phones and social media offer diverse content with a low barrier to entry, while games take more effort to get started.
how: Make sure the game's appeal is clear and strong enough to justify the effort of starting it.
example: People's free time going to phones and tablets.
quote: Games have a comparatively higher barrier to entry and take more effort to get started, so it'll be difficult if your game doesn't have the appeal to overcome that.
